questions.question: What is pocket money?
options: Money a child receives from their parents
Money a person must spend right away
Money a child receives from the bank to a children's account
Money that belongs to friends
questions.explanation: Pocket money is a set amount given by parents to help children learn about value.

questions.question: Pocket money is given to children so they learn to manage money.
questions.explanation: True - pocket money is a tool for learning how to make choices and handle a budget.

questions.question: If a child spends all their pocket money at once, the bank will give them more.
questions.explanation: False - money is finite. Once it is spent, you must wait for the next allowance.

questions.question: What is the best way to deal with pocket money?
options: Spend everything at once
Buy nothing
Divide the money between now and later
Only buy sweets
questions.explanation: Splitting money ensures you can enjoy something now while saving for the future.

questions.question: Chrumko has 10 euros. Sort each action into the correct category.
questions.explanation: Saving a portion ensures he has enough for his planned cinema trip, while spending a little now is fine.

questions.question: Chrumko buys a small thing and keeps the rest. Why?
options: Because he had no other option
So he will have money later as well
Because he did not want to buy anything
To spend less time in the shop
questions.explanation: Keeping the remainder allows for future purchases or emergencies.

questions.question: Chrumko gets his weekly pocket money and immediately wants to spend all of it on one big toy.
options: He should divide it between spending now and saving some for later.
He should spend it all right away since it's his money.
He should give it all to a friend.
He should wait for the bank to give him more if he runs out.
questions.explanation: The best way to deal with pocket money is to divide it between now and later, not spend everything at once.

questions.question: One of these statements is wrong. Find it.
options: Pocket money is money a child receives from their parents.
Pocket money is given to children so they learn to manage money.
If a child spends all their pocket money at once, the bank will simply give them more.
questions.explanation: Money is finite - once pocket money is spent, you must wait for the next allowance, the bank won't just give more.

questions.question: It is always a good idea to spend all your money at once.
questions.explanation: False - dividing money helps maintain financial security over time.

questions.question: Why do we divide our money?
options: So we have more things
So we have money for later as well
So we cannot enjoy life too much
So we do not have to count it
questions.explanation: It prevents running out of funds before the next income.

questions.question: Match each action to what it teaches you.
questions.explanation: Dividing money builds skills of planning, decision-making, and thinking ahead.
matchRight: Running out before the week ends

questions.question: Chrumko puts aside 7 euros from 10 euros. Why?
options: So he never uses them
Because he cannot spend it
Because he does not like shopping
So he can buy something else later
questions.explanation: Saving 7 euros creates a budget for a future goal.

questions.question: Put Chrumko's steps in the correct order - from receiving money to enjoying pizza.
questions.explanation: The pizza is the reward for his successful planning and saving.
orderItems: He puts aside most of the money
He tries not to spend the remaining money on impulse
Finally, he buys the pizza he's been craving

questions.question: Chrumko receives 10 euros and wants to buy pizza with friends in a few days, but also feels like spending everything today.
options: He should spend all 10 euros today since he has it now.
He should put most of it aside so he has enough for the pizza later.
He should ask his friends to pay for him.
He should throw away the money since dividing it is too hard.
questions.explanation: Chrumko puts aside most of his money so he has enough saved for pizza with friends later, rather than spending it all right away.

questions.question: One of these statements is wrong. Find it.
options: Dividing money helps you have money for later as well.
Dividing money builds skills of planning and decision-making.
It is always a good idea to spend all your money at once.
questions.explanation: Spending everything at once is not a good idea - dividing money helps maintain financial security over time.

questions.question: What does the decision "now vs later" mean?
options: To choose between two shops
To decide whether to spend the money now or keep it for later
To buy more things now and fewer things later
To not spend money at all
questions.explanation: It is the choice between immediate satisfaction and future benefit.

questions.question: Saving money means you can sometimes buy something bigger later.
questions.explanation: True - saving small amounts over time adds up to a larger sum for better items.

questions.question: Sort each behaviour into the correct group.
questions.explanation: Patience and planning prevent impulse buying and help reach bigger goals.
dragLabels: Grabbing the first thing you see

dragTargets.label: Impulsive
correctItems: Grabbing the first thing you see

questions.question: It is always a good idea to buy the first thing you see.
questions.explanation: False - thinking first helps you decide if you actually need the item.

questions.question: Chrumko does not buy a lollipop even though he wants it. Why?
options: He does not like sweets
Because he wanted it
He wants to buy something bigger later
He forgot
questions.explanation: He is practising delayed gratification for a bigger goal.

questions.question: Put the steps of Chrumko's decision in the correct order.
questions.explanation: Planning allowed him to get a more lasting item than a simple sweet.
orderItems: Chrumko sees the lollipop and wants it
He stops and thinks about his goal
He decides to wait and not buy it
He later buys the colouring book

questions.question: Chrumko sees a lollipop he really wants, but he's also saving for a colouring book he loves.
options: He should buy the lollipop immediately since he wants it now.
He should stop, think about his goal, and decide to wait so he can buy the colouring book later.
He should buy both no matter the cost.
He should give up on the colouring book entirely.
questions.explanation: Chrumko stops and thinks about his goal, then decides to wait, which lets him buy the colouring book later instead of a quick lollipop.

questions.question: One of these statements is wrong. Find it.
options: Saving money means you can sometimes buy something bigger later.
Thinking before buying is a patient and planned behaviour.
It is always a good idea to buy the first thing you see.
questions.explanation: It is not always a good idea to buy the first thing you see - thinking first helps you decide if you actually need it.

questions.question: Why is it good to plan what we will use our money for?
options: So we spend it faster
So we avoid unnecessary purchases
So we have fewer things
So we do not have to think
questions.explanation: Planning reduces waste and ensures money goes toward what matters.

questions.question: Spending money without thinking can mean you run out when you really need it.
questions.explanation: True - impulse spending often leads to a lack of funds for necessities.

questions.question: Match each situation to its outcome.
questions.explanation: Planning helps balance current needs with future desires.

questions.question: Chrumko wants ice cream and glasses. What should he do?
options: Spend everything right away
Buy ice cream and put the rest aside for the glasses
Buy only one thing without thinking
Buy two scoops of ice cream and then a whole box to take home
questions.explanation: This compromise satisfies a current craving while progressing toward a goal.

questions.question: Put Chrumko's steps in the correct order - from wanting glasses to buying them.
questions.explanation: Prioritising needs over immediate wants helps achieve goals faster.
orderItems: He won't spend the money he's saved
After one week he has enough to buy the glasses

questions.question: Chrumko wants ice cream today, but he's also saving for new glasses he needs.
options: He should spend everything on ice cream and forget about the glasses.
He should buy the ice cream and put the rest of his money aside for the glasses.
He should buy only ice cream every day until the glasses appear by themselves.
He should stop wanting ice cream completely.
questions.explanation: This compromise lets him enjoy a small treat now while still progressing toward his goal of getting glasses.

questions.question: One of these statements is wrong. Find it.
options: Planning helps you avoid unnecessary purchases.
Spending money without thinking can mean you run out when you really need it.
Saving consistently each week means you will never have enough for your goal.
questions.explanation: Saving consistently each week is exactly how Chrumko ends up with enough money for his goal, not the opposite.

questions.question: It is completely normal for a child to make a mistake when spending money.
questions.explanation: True - everyone makes mistakes; the important part is learning from them.

questions.question: What do financial mistakes help us learn?
options: How to spend more
How to avoid money
How to get rid of money faster
How to decide better
questions.explanation: Mistakes show us the consequences of poor planning.

questions.question: Put the steps for learning from a financial mistake in the correct order.
questions.explanation: Reflection is how we improve our money management skills.
orderItems: Notice that the item was not really needed
Feel a little regret about the choice
Make a better decision next time

questions.question: Match each behaviour to its result.
questions.explanation: Regret usually comes from realising the money could have been used better.

questions.question: Chrumko buys something he later does not use. What does that mean?
options: He made a good decision
It was a financial mistake
He had to buy it
The thing changed
questions.explanation: Buying unused items is a waste of resources.

questions.question: Sort each action into the correct category - what Chrumko SHOULD do vs SHOULD NOT do after a mistake.
questions.explanation: Slowing down and reflecting prevents repeating the same mistake.
dragLabels: Repeat the mistake to be sure
Decide even more quickly next time

dragTargets.label: Chrumko should NOT do this
correctItems: Repeat the mistake to be sure
Decide even more quickly next time

questions.question: Chrumko realizes he bought a toy last week that he never used and now regrets it.
options: He should repeat the same mistake next time to be sure it was wrong.
He should never spend any money ever again.
He should reflect on what went wrong and think more before buying next time.
He should decide even faster next time without thinking.
questions.explanation: Reflecting on the mistake and thinking more carefully next time is how you learn to make better decisions.

questions.question: One of these statements is wrong. Find it.
options: It is completely normal for a child to make a mistake when spending money.
Financial mistakes help us learn how to decide better.
Repeating the same financial mistake on purpose is a good way to learn.
questions.explanation: Repeating a mistake means you are not learning - reflecting on what went wrong is what actually helps you improve.
